cards.explanation: The answer is without blemish. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron the priest to take a young bull and a ram, “…both without blemish…” (Leviticus 9:2). One rule covers both animals. That's a high bar, friends. I can't keep my own apron spotless through one batch of chocolate chip dough.

The reason is that today the LORD will appear to them. Moses gives Aaron this line to pass on: “For today the LORD will appear to you.” (Leviticus 9:3-4). That's the whole reason, and it's a big one. I think you'd bring your best too if you knew the LORD was about to show up.

The answer is False. Leviticus 9:5 says, “…the whole congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.” It's not a private meeting for Aaron and the elders. The whole congregation is there. If this were my bakery, that's a line out the door and around the cookie planet.

The answer is True. Moses tells Aaron to sacrifice his own sin offering and burnt offering to make atonement for Aaron and for the people (Leviticus 9:7). So Aaron's offerings reach past Aaron. Then Moses adds the people's offering, which is also to make atonement for them.

The answer is horns. Aaron's sons bring him the blood, and he dips his finger in it and applies it to the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9). The rest he pours out at the base of the altar. I think dipping a finger with that much riding on it takes a steady hand, and mine would be shaking.

The answer is outside the camp. The fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver go up in smoke on the altar, but the flesh and the hide get burned up outside the camp (Leviticus 9:10-11). So one calf ends up in two places. Same calf, two addresses.

The answer is False. Aaron's sons bring him the burnt offering “…piece by piece, including the head…” (Leviticus 9:13). Then Aaron burns them on the altar. It's a team job, and his sons are doing the carrying.

The answer is True. Leviticus 9:14 says, “He washed the entrails and the legs and burned them atop the burnt offering on the altar.” The washing comes first, then the burning. Even in the middle of all this, there's a step for washing.

The answer is True. Aaron took the people's male goat, slaughtered it, and “…offered it for sin like the first one.” (Leviticus 9:15). The first one was his own sin offering. So he does the same job again, this time for the people. That's the same job twice in one day. I'm tired just saying it.

The answer is False. Aaron took a handful of the grain offering and burned it on the altar, in addition to the morning's burnt offering (Leviticus 9:17). Only a handful, not the whole thing. The text doesn't say what becomes of the rest.

The answer is on the breasts. Aaron's sons bring the fat portions from the ox and the ram, and the text says they “…placed these on the breasts.” (Leviticus 9:19-20). Only after that does Aaron burn the fat portions on the altar. It's the kind of careful order I wish I'd kept in my own kitchen. I once stamped a whole tray before I rolled the dough out.

The answer is that he waves them before the LORD. Aaron “…waved the breasts and the right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses had commanded.” (Leviticus 9:21). The fat is burned on the altar, and these get waved. Moses had commanded it, and Aaron does what Moses said.

The answer is that he lifts up his hands and blesses them. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22). He had made the sin offering, the burnt offering and the peace offering, and then he stepped down. The blessing comes right as he finishes. I think that's a lovely way to close it out.
The answer is False. “Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 9:23). The two of them go in together. Then they come out and bless the people. It's more fun with two, I'd say.

The answer is the burnt offering and the fat portions. Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed “…the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar.” (Leviticus 9:24). The fire comes from the LORD's presence. When all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown. I think that moment is one to stand still and take in.

The answer is True. “…when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown.” (Leviticus 9:24). The whole crowd sees the fire and shouts for joy. I think I'd be loud too. I get loud when a batch comes out right.
